Friday's close (Fri Nov 20) was a broad risk-off session led by tech. The Nasdaq Composite fell -5.28% (-1,261.47) to 22,617.73, the S&P 500 fell -3.70% (-265.44) to 6,910.39, the Dow fell -1.93%, the Russell 2000 fell -2.76%, and the Nikkei fell -5.06%. The VIX jumped +7.45 to 35.89. US Info Tech lost -7.11% on the day, -12.16% on the week and -17.81% over the month. Treasuries rallied hard as a haven: the 2Y fell 11.49bp to 4.6469% and the 10Y fell 10.23bp to 4.9438%. Gold (-2.40%) and silver (-4.16%) were sold with everything else, which looks like de-risking or liquidation rather than a classic flight to safety. The bigger story is credit. US HY OAS widened +23bp to 3.67%. The HY contagion panel shows the Caa-B gap at 800bp, in the 99.84th percentile of the past 5 years, with Caa at 1,174bp (100th 5y pctl) and spreads at their widest since 2020-04-15. The stress is no longer confined to CCCs: single-B widened +63bp in a week and +49bp in a month (to 374bp), Ba widened +39bp on the week (to 221bp), and IG widened +10bp (to 96bp). The 63-day Caa/B correlation has climbed to 0.68, from 0.35 three months ago, back to its 5y median of 0.69. That says the moves are increasingly shared rather than isolated. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. The AI-credit backstop read is the sharpest piece. CoreWeave 5Y CDS rose +155bp day-on-day to 1,324.93bp, which is 130bp ABOVE the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record and 117.6% of the June-low-to-record run. Nvidia CDS widened +25.57bp to 149.38bp and Oracle +23.37bp to 348.22bp. Nvidia stock fell -22.92% on the week and sits -47.53% from its 52-week high. On this data the market is not buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds: the guarantor's own credit is now being repriced alongside them. CDX IG (65.157) and CDX HY (385.61) are in their 98.8th and 99.2nd 1-year percentiles. Note that the tech-analog signpost uses a different CoreWeave reading (1,183.49bp, just under the record), so the two snapshots disagree on timing. The tech phase model still places the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm). However, four signposts are now triggered: VIX above 30, VXN at 45.25 vs 35, breadth (78.6% of basket names more than 20% off their highs), and SOX -42.5% from its 52-week high. Its 6-month Phase 2+3 odds rose 25.7pp vs Nov 19, and the phase model puts 3-month odds at 49.9% Phase 2 / 16.0% Phase 3 / 34.0% Phase 4. These are model estimates. Sentiment is fearful: AAII bull-minus-bear is -8.9, and the rally-watch 'VIX turn' condition is not yet met (35.9 vs the 32.3 needed).

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.26 vol points (3th percentile of the 74 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 106.3 (77th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 70bp (flatter by 22bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (122bp above today).

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 51 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 64/100 — Sticky and slightly re-accelerating at the core, not a re-ignition. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score sits in the upper part of its historical range, with median CPI, trimmed-mean CPI and core sticky CPI all flagged 'rising'. Median and trimmed-mean PCE are flat. Breadth is mixed: per the Dallas Fed distribution, 16.6% of the PCE basket is inflating above 10% and 10.2% at 5-10%, while 25.6% is falling. Price pressure is concentrated (flexible CPI 6.2%, consistent with energy and the Iran shock), not universal. Markets are not pricing persistence: 5y breakeven 2.1934% and 1y 1.829%. That gap is a risk if oil stays high. The persistence score of 64 is an analyst estimate.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
7 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 6 beyond 2000 — 52/100
On valuation, today is far from the March-2000 peak. Nasdaq trailing P/E of 36.16x is 13% of the way to the 175x peak, SOX P/E of 28.84x is 22%, and the Nasdaq stretch vs its 200DMA has gone to 0% (it now trades -10.1% below). The Late-cycle Catalyst and Macro Regime dimensions look much more 2000-like. IG (120%) and Baa-10y (144%) tightness, the NFCI (151%) and commodities-vs-equities (200%) are all at or beyond 2000-peak conditions, and the curve is at 70%. Credit complacency, not equity froth, was the 2000-style excess, and that complacency is now unwinding fast at the bottom of the ratings ladder. Bear-market signposts have flipped: VIX complacency 0% and AAII 27%. The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 33 days from the 2026-10-06 peak. The basket drawdown of -30.31% is already deeper than the -22.85% the 2000 basket showed on the same day. The phase model puts 1-month odds at 75.5% Phase 2 and 79.5% ever reaching Phase 2+. At 3 months it puts 49.9% P2 / 16.0% P3 / 34.0% P4, and at 12 months 67.2% P4 (trough/recovery). These are model estimates, not certainties. The defensive dial is Step 1, Cautious (since 2026-11-05; live from 2026-12-01).

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (36x) ≈ 21% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

This does not look like 2000 on price multiples, because the bubble was never as extreme in earnings-adjusted terms. The bust mechanics look familiar, though. Leadership concentrated in AI infrastructure (semis, neoclouds, Oracle) has broken: SOX is -42.5% from its high, SMH -40.19%, Nvidia -47.53%, CoreWeave -71.37%, IREN -82.58%. Credit, which was priced for perfection (IG and Baa-10y tighter than 2000), is the transmission channel. The 2000 analog says Phase 2 begins when credit stress leaves the speculative fringe. HY OAS (344bp in the model's reading) is 76bp from the 5y-80th-pct trigger, and CoreWeave CDS is around its record. The HMM regime still reads 98.1% 'Calm (Phase-1-like)' and the credit regime 97.3% 'Credit calm'. Those are lagging confirmations against the contagion data in the HY panel. The economy has not cracked (Sahm 0.0, ISM 55.5, C&I charge-offs 0.58%), which limits the Phase 3 path for now. The model's historical tilt favours gold, Treasury duration and cash over mega-cap growth, developed international and EM. The five headline inputs (top-10 concentration ~36%, IPO froth 45/100, CAPE ~35x, market cap/GDP ~195%, LT EPS growth expectations 60/100) are analyst estimates, not sourced or computed figures. The IPO-froth estimate leans on Anthropic's reported November listing.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and cash, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

December FOMC: a 25bp hike is the base case from reporting, now with less conviction (inference). After October's hold at 3.75-4.00%, reports said a December hike was left squarely on the table, with ~88% odds priced and two dissents in favour of an immediate hike. Warsh named October and December as his decision points and declined to pre-commit. Since then the 2Y yield has dropped 11.49bp in one day and credit is cracking, so a hike is less certain. A hawkish hold is a realistic alternative (inference, not sourced).

~1 YEAR

Inferred from his record and stated framework: Warsh is a rules-minded hawk on inflation credibility who favours a smaller balance sheet and less forward guidance. He is also open to the view that AI-driven productivity is disinflationary. Over ~12 months, expect policy to tighten modestly or stay flat while core PCE is around 3.12%. Cuts would come only if the credit/equity unwind tips the labour data (currently unemployment 4.1%, claims 203k, Sahm 0.0). A reported move to a 'six plus two' meeting schedule would mean fewer scheduled decisions. All of this is inference from sources, not on-record guidance.

Warsh's public line is not to prejudge meetings and to weigh output, jobs and inflation at named decision points. Commentators note that his heavy communication has barely moved December hike pricing. Earlier 2026 analysis, such as PIMCO's view that he could deliver two cuts, now looks outdated given the hike pricing. The tension for December: sticky core inflation (core PCE 3.12%, rising sticky CPI) argues for a hike, while a -5% Nasdaq day, VIX at 35.89 and contagion in junk credit argue for patience. Markets will read his December decision as a test of whether a 'Warsh put' exists.

Sources: Portfolio Adviser — Warsh sticks to the script as Fed holds rates but December hike highly likely · investingLive — Fed chair Warsh talks up a storm but December rate hike bets barely budge · investingLive — Warsh won't prejudge rest of 2026, names October and December as decision points · PIMCO — Under a Warsh Fed, expect a thoughtful policy approach · CFR — Why Kevin Warsh won't revolutionize the Federal Reserve
